title: Hyperosmolar Hyperglycaemic State (HHS)
clinicalScenario: Outline only. Planned scope: Recognition, cautious fluid replacement, insulin timing, osmolality and sodium monitoring, thrombosis risk, precipitant search. Candidate sources to verify: JBDS-IP management of HHS in adults; ADA/EASD hyperglycaemic crises consensus.

evidenceAudit.scope: Adult (over 18 years) Emergency Department (ED) recognition and first 24 hours of management of Hyperosmolar Hyperglycaemic State (HHS), based on the Joint British Diabetes Societies (JBDS) 2022 guideline, with the Saudi Ministry of Health (MOH) diabetes emergencies protocol and a review of the 2024 international consensus shown side by side where they differ.
findings: Full protocol rebuilt from the source dossier opened on 2026-10-21; exact source locations are recorded in each investigation and medicine row.
The original outline remains preserved; this additive version is non-current and pending clinical review.
unverifiedSections: Normal reference ranges are typical adult values, not taken from the cited guidelines; ranges differ between laboratories.
Symptoms, examination signs, differentials, precipitants and the pathophysiology bullets are standard clinical content and were not extracted line by line from the opened sources.
JBDS page numbers were inferred from extracted footers and may be off by one; the executive summary says "most people" should receive LMWH while the body text says everyone unless contraindicated.

The JBDS text gives an example fluid rate for people under 50 kg or with heart or renal disease that could not be confirmed, so no number is given here; the dose for 0.45% sodium chloride is not stated in the opened text.
The 2024 consensus was read through a 2025 review article, not the primary report; the Saudi MOH protocol is undated and its insulin timing rules differ from JBDS.
Registration with the Saudi Food and Drug Authority (SFDA) was not checked for any drug.
At 40 mmol/L potassium chloride in fluid at 500 mL/hour the potassium rate is 20 mmol/hour (derived); JBDS gives no maximum potassium rate or central-line requirement.
The weight table above 140 kg were not given in the opened JBDS text. JBDS Appendix 1 says 'made up to 50 mL'. JBDS page numbers follow the contents page and may not match printed pages.
The potassium below 3.5 mmol/L row borrows the level rule from a Worcestershire guideline past its review date; JBDS gives only senior review.

The enoxaparin dose is from the manufacturer's international package insert (Sanofi India, CCDS version 14), not the Saudi SFDA label; the 20 mg renal dose applies below 30 mL/min creatinine clearance.

Renal, hepatic and age adjustments for the drugs added in this revision are from manufacturer labels (UK Summary of Product Characteristics, US prescribing information and a New Zealand data sheet), not from Saudi Food and Drug Authority labels.

pathophysiology.summary: HHS is severe hyperglycaemia with marked dehydration and high plasma osmolality but little or no ketosis or acidosis.
keyMechanisms: Relative insulin deficiency is enough to cause high glucose but suppresses fat breakdown, so ketone production stays low.
Very high glucose causes a prolonged osmotic diuresis and a large fluid deficit.
Rising osmolality draws water out of brain cells, which lowers conscious level.
Falling glucose or sodium too fast during treatment can shift water into the brain and risks cerebral oedema or central pontine myelinolysis.
Hyperosmolar blood and dehydration raise the risk of thrombosis.

symptoms: Days of increasing thirst, passing large volumes of urine and weakness.
physicalSigns: Marked dehydration with tachycardia and low blood pressure.
Reduced conscious level in severe cases.
Foot pressure damage or ulceration in people who are drowsy or immobile.
redFlags: Potassium below 3.5 or above 6.0 mmol/L on admission.
Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score below 12 or an abnormal Alert, Voice, Pain, Unresponsive (AVPU) score.
Systolic Blood Pressure (SBP) below 90 mmHg, oxygen saturation below 92% on air or urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/hour.
Creatinine above 200 µmol/L and/or Acute Kidney Injury (AKI); hypothermia; myocardial infarction or stroke.
precipitants: Infection, particularly pneumonia or urinary tract infection.
Acute vascular events such as myocardial infarction or stroke.
Medicines that raise glucose or cause fluid loss, such as steroids and diuretics.
Missed or insufficient diabetes treatment, or undiagnosed type 2 diabetes.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Ketones above 3.0 mmol/L with pH below 7.3 or bicarbonate below 15.0 mmol/L
Marked hyperosmolality together with pH below 7.3 and ketones above 3.0 mmol/L
Glucose is high but osmolality and dehydration are not in the HHS range

clinicalManagement.title: Immediate
actions: Confirm HHS with glucose, osmolality, ketones, pH and bicarbonate before starting; if pH is below 7.3 and ketones are above 3.0 mmol/L, treat as DKA or mixed DKA and HHS.
Give 0.9% sodium chloride 1 L over the first hour; go faster if SBP is below 90 mmHg.
Do not start insulin early unless ketones are above 1.0 mmol/L (see Medicines).
Measure hourly: glucose, sodium, potassium, urea and osmolality for the first 6 hours, and ketones until resolved.
Check GCS or neurological status every 1–2 hours; keep a fluid balance chart with a minimum urine output of 0.5 mL/kg/hour.
Protect the feet: assume high risk, off-load heels and check daily.

clinicalManagement.title: Ongoing
actions: From 60 minutes to 6 hours give a further 0.5–1 L/hour of 0.9% sodium chloride, aiming for a positive balance of 2–3 L by 6 hours and 3–6 L by 12 hours.

Keep sodium change within 10 mmol/L per 24 hours, the fall in osmolality at 3.0–8.0 mOsm/kg per hour and the fall in glucose no more than 5.0 mmol/L per hour; reduce fluid and/or insulin if osmolality falls faster than 8.0 mOsm/kg per hour.
Use 0.45% sodium chloride only if osmolality is not falling despite adequate 0.9% sodium chloride.
Use more cautious fluid replacement in people under 50 kg and in heart or renal disease.

Give prophylactic Low Molecular Weight Heparin (LMWH), enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously once daily (20 mg if creatinine clearance is below 30 mL/min), for the whole admission unless contraindicated; therapeutic anticoagulation only for suspected thrombosis or acute coronary syndrome.
After the first 6 hours, if the response is satisfactory, move glucose, sodium, potassium and urea to 2-hourly checks.
HHS is resolved when osmolality is below 300 mOsm/kg, hypovolaemia is corrected (urine output at least 0.5 mL/kg/hour), cognition is back to pre-morbid state and glucose is below 15 mmol/L.

clinicalManagement.title: Escalation
actions: Any red-flag marker above (for example osmolality above 350 mOsm/kg, sodium above 160 mmol/L, pH below 7.1, GCS below 12, SBP below 90 mmHg) means HDU or Level 2 care.
Mixed DKA and HHS: treat using the DKA pathway at 0.1 units/kg/hour.
Osmolality falling too fast or sodium changing faster than 10 mmol/L per 24 hours: reduce fluid and/or insulin and seek senior advice.

regimens.indication: Stop ketone production and lower glucose
regimens.genericName: Human soluble insulin 1 unit/mL infusion (50 units in 50 mL 0.9% sodium chloride)
regimens.dose: Start immediately at 0.05 units/kg/hour. Rate by weight at 0.05 units/kg/hour: 50–59 kg = 2.5 units/hour; 60–69 = 3; 70–79 = 3.5; 80–89 = 4; 90–99 = 4.5; 100–109 = 5; 110–119 = 5.5; 120–129 = 6; 130–139 = 6.5; under 50 kg or over 140 kg needs senior or Diabetes Specialist Team (DST) advice. Reduce the rate by 50% if glucose falls by more than 5.0 mmol/L per hour; in the 12–24 hour phase adjust by 1 unit/hour each hour
regimens.route: IV infusion by syringe pump. Preparation: draw 50 units of human soluble insulin (Actrapid) with an insulin syringe (never an IV syringe) and make up to 50 mL with 0.9% sodium chloride = 1 unit/mL; run glucose and insulin in the same line through a three-way non-return valve
regimens.duration: Until ketones, glucose and osmolality targets are met (resolution: osmolality below 300 mOsm/kg, urine output 0.5 mL/kg/hour or more, back to usual cognition, glucose below 15 mmol/L)
contraindications: glucose falling faster than 5.0 mmol/L per hour

learningObjectives: Recognise HHS and separate it from DKA and mixed disease.
Replace fluid slowly and monitor sodium, osmolality and glucose hourly.
Know when insulin is started and when to escalate.
pitfalls: Giving a DKA dose of insulin (0.1 units/kg/hour) to a person with HHS.
Lowering glucose or sodium too fast, which risks cerebral oedema.
Treating a rising sodium early in treatment as a reason to switch to hypotonic fluid.
Missing a mixed DKA and HHS picture.
keyPoints: HHS is treated mainly with fluid; insulin is started early only if ketones are above 1.0 mmol/L.
Keep sodium change within 10 mmol/L per 24 hours and glucose fall within 5.0 mmol/L per hour.
Give LMWH and protect the feet.

dischargeCriteria: HHS resolved (osmolality below 300 mOsm/kg, glucose below 15 mmol/L, normal cognition, adequate urine output) and eating and drinking.
Diabetes education done and a written care plan copied to the General Practitioner (GP).
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Diabetes Specialist Team (DST) review within one working day and before discharge. Follow-up by the diabetes team or primary care after discharge; most people go home on subcutaneous insulin.
